questions.prompt: A minimum-phase loop gain holds a slope of \(-40\ \mathrm{dB}\) per decade across a wide band around crossover. About what phase does that slope imply?
options: about \(0^\circ\), because phase is set by the gain at one frequency, not by the slope
questions.explanation: For a minimum-phase frequency response, a slope of \(-20n\ \mathrm{dB}\) per decade, held over a wide band, corresponds to a phase near \(-90n\) degrees. Here \(n = 2\), so the phase is near \(-180^\circ\). A single pole (\(n = 1\)) would be near \(-90^\circ\), and three poles near \(-270^\circ\). The phase tracks the slope, not the absolute gain. The rule fails if the system has a right-half-plane zero or a delay: those add lag the magnitude plot does not show.

questions.prompt: A pure delay of \(0.02\ \mathrm{s}\) has frequency response \(e^{-j\omega T}\). What is its phase lag at \(\omega = 50\ \mathrm{rad/s}\), in degrees? Give a positive number.
questions.explanation:
The phase is \(-\omega T\) radians. \(\omega T = 50 \times 0.02 = 1\) radian, and \(1 \times 180/\pi = 57.2958\) degrees of lag. The magnitude of a delay is \(1\) at every frequency, so a magnitude plot cannot see this lag.
• \(50 \times 0.02 = 1\) leaves the answer in radians.
• \(0.02 \times 180/\pi = 1.15\) forgets to multiply by \(\omega\).
• \(360 \times 0.02 = 7.2\) treats the delay as a fraction of a one-second period.

questions.prompt: You may multiply a transfer function by one of the following without changing its magnitude Bode plot. Which choice adds phase lag?
options: Multiplying by \(s+z\) for \(z>0\), a new left-half-plane zero
Multiplying by a positive constant gain
Multiplying by \(\dfrac{s+z}{z-s}\) and then taking the magnitude only
questions.explanation: \((z-s)/(z+s)\) is an all-pass: its magnitude is \(1\) at every imaginary \(s = j\omega\), and its phase is \(-2\tan^{-1}(\omega/z)\), which is lag. A new left-half-plane zero \((s+z)\) raises the magnitude by \(20\ \mathrm{dB}\) per decade and adds phase lead, not lag. A positive constant changes the magnitude by a fixed number of decibels and adds no phase. Looking only at the magnitude of the reciprocal all-pass throws away exactly the phase the question is about.

questions.prompt: The all-pass \((7-s)/(7+s)\) is evaluated at \(\omega = 14\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). What is its phase, in degrees? Give the signed number.
questions.explanation:
At \(s = j14\), the numerator \(7-j14\) has angle \(\tan^{-1}(-14/7) = \tan^{-1}(-2)\), and the denominator \(7+j14\) has the opposite angle. The phase is \(-2\tan^{-1}(2) = -126.870\) degrees. Equivalently, a delay-free all-pass of this form contributes \(-2\tan^{-1}(\omega/z)\).
• \(-63.4\) degrees counts only one of the two factors.
• \(+126.9\) flips the sign, which would be lead.
• \(-90\) would be the phase at \(\omega = 7\), the corner, not at twice that frequency.

questions.prompt: Which transfer function is minimum phase?
questions.explanation: Minimum phase means every zero is in the open left half-plane and there is no time delay. \((s+3)/((s+1)(s+8))\) has its only zero at \(-3\). \((s-3)/((s+1)(s+8))\) has a zero at \(+3\). A factor \(e^{-0.1 s}\) is a delay, which adds lag at every frequency and is not minimum phase. \((3-s)/(s+3)\) is an all-pass with a right-half-plane zero.

questions.prompt: \(H(s) = \dfrac{s+5}{s+20}\). What is the phase of \(H(j5)\), in degrees? Give the signed number.
questions.explanation:
The zero at \(-5\) contributes \(\tan^{-1}(5/5) = 45^\circ\). The pole at \(-20\) contributes \(-\tan^{-1}(5/20) = -14.036^\circ\). The sum is \(+30.964\) degrees. Both factors are minimum phase, so the zero's lead is only partly cancelled by a pole that is still well above this frequency.
• \(45\) degrees keeps the zero and forgets the pole.
• \(-45\) degrees gives the zero the sign of a right-half-plane zero.
• \(14\) degrees is only the pole's contribution.

questions.prompt: \(H(s) = \dfrac{10}{s(s+10)}\). What is the phase of \(H(j1)\), in degrees? Give the signed number.
questions.explanation:
At \(s = j\), the denominator is \(j(10+j) = -1 + 10j\). The angle of \(-1+10j\) is \(\tan^{-1}(10/1)\) measured from the negative real axis, \(180^\circ - 84.289^\circ = 95.711^\circ\). The numerator is positive, so the phase of \(H\) is \(-95.711\) degrees. A pure \(1/s\) would contribute exactly \(-90^\circ\). The extra pole at \(-10\) has only begun to add lag at \(\omega = 1\).
• \(-90\) ignores the pole at \(-10\).
• \(-84.3\) uses \(	an^{-1}(10)\) with the wrong quadrant, as if the real part were positive.
• \(-180\) would be the high-frequency phase, two poles past both corners.

questions.prompt: A step response first moves opposite the direction it finally settles. Which feature produces that inverse response?
options: A left-half-plane zero, which adds a derivative kick of the same sign as the final value
Extra damping, which slows the rise but does not reverse it
A pure time delay, which shifts the whole response later
questions.explanation: A right-half-plane zero makes the high-frequency gain opposite in sign to the low-frequency gain, so the first motion opposes the final value. A left-half-plane zero can add an initial kick, but of the same sign as the settling value. Damping changes speed and overshoot, not the initial direction. A pure delay postpones the response and does not reverse it.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that starts at zero, dips below the axis, then climbs and settles above the axis.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the all-pass \((8-s)/(8+s)\) at \(\omega = 4\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). What is its phase, in degrees? Give the signed number.
questions.explanation:
The phase of \((z-s)/(z+s)\) on \(s = j\omega\) is \(-2\tan^{-1}(\omega/z)\). With \(\omega/z = 0.5\), \(\tan^{-1}(0.5) = 26.565^\circ\) and the phase is \(-53.130\) degrees. The magnitude is exactly \(1\), so this lag is invisible on a magnitude plot.
• \(-26.6\) degrees counts one factor.
• \(-90\) would require \(\omega = z\).
• \(+53.1\) is the phase of the minimum-phase mirror \((s+8)/(8)\), not of this all-pass.

questions.prompt: Replacing a left-half-plane zero at \(-12\) by a right-half-plane zero at \(+12\) multiplies the transfer function by the all-pass \((12-s)/(12+s)\). At \(\omega = 4\ \mathrm{rad/s}\), how much extra phase does that all-pass add, in degrees? Give the signed number.
questions.explanation:
The extra phase is \(-2\tan^{-1}(4/12) = -2\tan^{-1}(1/3) = -36.870\) degrees. That lag is the price of the right-half-plane zero at this frequency. It is a fundamental limit: the magnitude plot is unchanged, but phase margin shrinks, so the usable crossover has to stay well below the zero.
• \(-18.4\) degrees is a single \(	an^{-1}(1/3)\).
• \(-90\) is the all-pass phase at \(\omega = 12\), not at \(4\).
• \(+36.9\) would be lead, which a right-half-plane zero does not provide.

questions.prompt: A design plans to cross over at \(40\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) and must live with a \(5\ \mathrm{ms}\) delay. How many degrees of phase lag does that delay add at crossover? Give a positive number.
questions.explanation:
Lag is \(\omega T\) radians: \(40 \times 0.005 = 0.2\) radian, times \(180/\pi\), is \(11.459\) degrees. The delay does not change \(|L|\). It only spends phase margin. Keeping that lag small is one of the limits on how high the crossover can sit.
• \(0.2\) leaves the unit in radians.
• \(40/0.005 = 8000\) divides instead of multiplying.
• \(5\) is the delay in milliseconds, not the phase.

questions.prompt: A right-half-plane zero sits at \(+6\). Consider the factor \((6-s)\) alone. What is its phase, in degrees, at \(\omega = 6\ \mathrm{rad/s}\)? Give the signed number.
questions.explanation: \(6 - j6\) lies at angle \(\tan^{-1}(-6/6) = -45^\circ\). A left-half-plane zero at \(-6\) would have contributed \(+45^\circ\) at this frequency. The \(90^\circ\) gap between those two is the all-pass penalty at the zero's own frequency, and it is why an right-half-plane zero near crossover is expensive.
